title: A Credit-Card Rewards Founder From Bengaluru Just Got Handed WhatsApp's 3 Billion Users
excerpt: Meta is putting $900 million into CRED and naming Kunal Shah as WhatsApp's first Indian chief. The diaspora's most-used app now answers to a man who built his name on getting Indians to pay their bills on time.
body:
Mark Zuckerberg has spent a decade trying to make money from WhatsApp and mostly failing. His latest answer is to hand the app to a man who spent the past eight years persuading affluent Indians that paying a credit-card bill on time deserves a reward.

On June 22nd Meta named Kunal Shah, founder of the Bengaluru fintech CRED, as the new global head of WhatsApp. He succeeds Will Cathcart, who ran the service for seven years and is moving to a new product role inside Meta. Arriving with the appointment was a corporate sweetener: Meta is investing about $900 million in CRED for a minority stake of roughly 20%, valuing the loss-making-until-recently startup at $4.5 billion. Shah will relocate from Bengaluru to Menlo Park; CRED's finance chief Miten Sampat becomes interim CEO.

For the Indian diaspora, this is not an abstract boardroom reshuffle. It is a change of management at the single most-used piece of software in their lives.

The app the diaspora actually runs on

WhatsApp has more than three billion users, and India — with some 500 million of them — is its largest market by a wide margin. For NRIs the app is less a messenger than infrastructure: the video call to parents in Pune, the family group with forty cousins across three continents, the channel a Jersey City sari shop uses to take orders. When the person setting WhatsApp's roadmap is himself a Bengaluru founder who understands that texture, the product decisions are likely to bend toward India rather than treat it as an afterthought.

That cuts both ways. Analysts were blunt about why Shah, a payments man, got the job. WhatsApp's unsolved problem is monetization — it launched payments in India years ago to underwhelming uptake — and "India will be where most of the experimentation will happen," said Satish Meena of Datum Intelligence. Translation for the diaspora: the ads, paid tiers and commerce features tested on your relatives back home will arrive in your chats too, just later.

Why the deal is structured so carefully

The fine print betrays how sensitive this is. Meta is taking no board seat, is paying part of the price in ad credits, and has explicitly said it will not get access to CRED's customer data. India's central bank has long worried about American Big Tech dominating payments — UPI is already carved up between Walmart's PhonePe and Google Pay — and there are already calls to review the arrangement. Meta, in effect, is buying a foothold in Indian fintech while trying not to trip the regulator's wires.

For NRI investors, CRED's trajectory is the more tangible story. The company reported its first profitable quarter in 2026 and around $325 million in annual revenue across payments, lending, insurance and wealth. Shah's note marking the moment doubled as a pre-IPO pitch: 17 million members, four ESOP buybacks, a full stack of regulatory licences. With Razorpay and others already filing to list, CRED's Meta-blessed valuation is another data point for diaspora investors trying to price India's fintech cohort ahead of a listing wave.

A pattern, not an exception

Shah becomes the latest name on a roll-call that French president Emmanuel Macron once recited to make a point: the CEOs of Alphabet, Microsoft, IBM, Adobe and Palo Alto Networks are all of Indian origin. What is different here is the direction of travel. Pichai and Nadella climbed the corporate ladder inside American firms over decades. Shah built a company in India, sold a slice of it to an American giant, and parlayed that into running one of its crown-jewel products — without ever working his way up through Silicon Valley.

For an Indian engineer in the Bay Area, that is a subtly different aspiration. The path to the top of Big Tech no longer runs exclusively through a US graduate programme and twenty years of internal politics. It can also run through building something India can't live without, then trading it up. Whether Shah can finally make WhatsApp pay is the question Zuckerberg is spending nearly a billion dollars to answer. The diaspora will be the first to feel the result.
